The plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, which spreads among rodents and can be transmitted to humans through fleas. Both bubonic and pneumonic plague are fatal if not treated early.

Since the 1990s, most human cases have been reported in Africa, especially Congo and Madagascar. In the U.S., there are an average of about seven human cases per year, mostly in rural areas of the American West. http://www.bing.com/news/apiclick.aspx?r.summary_en: The plague, a rare bacterial infection that killed tens of millions in 14th-century Europe, still exists today. According to WHO, most human cases since the 1990s have been reported in Africa, particularly Congo and Madagascar. The CDC reports an average of about seven human cases annually in the U.S., mostly in rural western areas. Recently, a worker at a plague research institute in Siberia died of pneumonia, prompting quarantine of the facility, though tests showed no plague evidence. The plague, caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria, exists in three forms: bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic. It spreads through infected fleas bites or contact with infected animals. When treated early with antibiotics, the plague can be cured.
